title: Other Ways of Talking About the Future
summary: Use precise expressions of imminence, expected timing, likelihood and intention to describe future events. Distinguish due to + infinitive from due to + noun, recognise past perspectives on future intentions and choose shall only where its register is appropriate.
learningObjectives: Choose on the verge of, on the brink of and on the point of with a noun or -ing form to convey imminent developments and their connotations.
Differentiate be due to + infinitive for an expected event, be bound or sure to for high likelihood and be set to for readiness or an anticipated development.
Express intentions with verbs such as aim, intend, propose and resolve, including natural progressive forms and be looking to + infinitive.
Backshift these intentions from a past viewpoint and assess when shall or shan’t is appropriate rather than ordinary will or won’t.

explanation.heading: Approaching a change: on the verge, brink or point of
explanation.body: Be on the verge of, be on the brink of and be on the point of take a noun or an -ing verb. They suggest that a change or action is close, but they do not establish that it actually happens. On the brink of often highlights a significant, potentially troubling or dramatic development; on the point of commonly refers to an immediate personal action. All three also work from a past viewpoint with was or were.
explanation.example: The theatre is on the verge of closing unless a new sponsor can be found.

explanation.heading: Expected time, strong likelihood and readiness
explanation.body: Be due to + infinitive conveys an event expected at a particular time. Be sure to and be bound to express confidence that something will happen; be set to can indicate readiness or a development widely expected to happen. Be due to + noun or -ing is different: it introduces a cause, not a scheduled future action. Existential there can precede sure or bound to, as in There is bound to be a delay, but not normally be due or be set to in this pattern.
explanation.example: The coastal ferry is due to arrive at noon, but it is bound to be late if the winds become stronger.

explanation.heading: Stating an intention with a to-infinitive
explanation.body: Verbs such as aim, intend, plan, expect, hope, propose, resolve and promise can be followed by a to-infinitive to refer to an intended or anticipated action. With many of these verbs, either a present simple or present continuous form is possible, with the continuous often emphasising a current or developing plan. Certain verbs impose their own usage restrictions, so the forms should not be treated as freely interchangeable in every context.
explanation.example: We intend to update the visitor guide in spring, and we are aiming to publish it before the holiday season.

explanation.heading: Looking to do something and intentions viewed from the past
explanation.body: Be looking to + infinitive is frequently used to describe plans or aims, especially in business, news and organisational announcements. Using past tenses with these expressions places the future in relation to an earlier viewpoint. Was due to, was hoping to and had resolved to refer to what was expected or intended then, without necessarily telling us whether the action took place.
explanation.example: The gallery had planned to extend its opening hours, but the proposal was later withdrawn.

explanation.heading: Shall and shan’t: restricted modern uses
explanation.body: In current everyday affirmative and negative future statements, will and won’t are considerably more common than shall and shan’t, even with I or we. Shall or shan’t may still be heard with I or we in more formal or traditional speech. Shall with other subjects is mostly found in formal rules, contracts or literary language, rather than as an ordinary neutral future. This is separate from the common suggestion form Shall we ...?, which has its own communicative function.
explanation.example: We will send the details tomorrow; the organisers shall retain the right to alter the programme.

comparisons.title: A scheduled future event versus its cause

left.label: Due to + infinitive: expected timing
left.example: The ferry is due to leave at seven.
left.note: Is due to leave says when departure is expected.

right.label: Due to + noun: reason
right.example: The ferry is delayed due to thick fog.
right.note: Due to thick fog explains why the delay happened.

left.label: Bound to: confident forecast
left.example: The revised plan is bound to attract questions.
left.note: The speaker regards the questions as highly likely.

right.label: Looking to: proposed goal
right.example: The team is looking to attract new supporters.
right.note: The team intends to achieve the result; success is not guaranteed.

examples.sentence: The small museum is on the brink of losing its only public grant.
examples.note: On the brink of + -ing presents a significant threatened development as very near.

examples.sentence: The panel is due to publish its findings on Wednesday.
examples.note: Is due to + infinitive conveys an expected scheduled announcement.

examples.sentence: There is sure to be a lively discussion after the documentary.
examples.note: There is sure to be predicts the existence of an event with high confidence.

examples.sentence: The research centre is looking to recruit more volunteers next summer.
examples.note: Is looking to recruit presents an organisational intention, not a completed outcome.

examples.sentence: The exhibition was set to open in May, but repairs forced a postponement.
examples.note: Was set to expresses an earlier expectation that was not fulfilled on schedule.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The actress was on the point to announce the winner.
commonMistakes.correct: The actress was on the point of announcing the winner.
commonMistakes.why: On the point of needs of followed by a noun or -ing form.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The conference is due opening at ten tomorrow.
commonMistakes.correct: The conference is due to open at ten tomorrow.
commonMistakes.why: For an expected scheduled event, due takes to + base infinitive.

commonMistakes.incorrect: There is bound be some disagreement at the meeting.
commonMistakes.correct: There is bound to be some disagreement at the meeting.
commonMistakes.why: Bound requires to + infinitive, including in the existential there construction.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The council is looking to improving the waterfront.
commonMistakes.correct: The council is looking to improve the waterfront.
commonMistakes.why: Looking to expresses intention and takes the base infinitive, not an -ing form.

studyTips: Classify future statements by meaning: imminence, expected schedule, confident prediction or active intention; then choose one matching expression.
Write one past-viewpoint sentence using was due to and another using had intended to; add a second clause clarifying whether the plan occurred.
Compare a neutral sentence with will with a contract-style sentence using shall; identify why their registers differ.

exercises.prompt: A scientist predicts that the team is very likely to find more evidence. Choose the phrase expressing high likelihood.
exercises.feedback: Is bound to + base verb expresses a strong expectation about a future outcome.

exercises.prompt: A scheduled inspection is expected at 8 a.m. Which sentence correctly reports the time?
choices: The inspector is due to arrive at eight.
The inspector is due arriving at eight.
The inspector is due of arriving at eight.
exercises.feedback: Is due to arrive states the expected time of a future event.

exercises.prompt: A committee intends to recruit volunteers in the coming year. Which sentence naturally expresses its current organisational aim?
choices: The committee is looking recruit volunteers.
The committee is looking to recruiting volunteers.
The committee is looking to recruit volunteers.
exercises.feedback: Is looking to recruit is a standard construction for an organisational intention.

exercises.prompt: Choose the conventional style for a neutral everyday prediction about tomorrow.
exercises.feedback: Will improve is the normal neutral future prediction; shall is not ordinary with the weather.

exercises.prompt: The orchestra ___ (on the verge / announce) a national tour. Write the complete is-form phrase.
acceptedAnswers: is on the verge of announcing
exercises.feedback: On the verge of takes an -ing form to suggest a near announcement.

exercises.prompt: The award ceremony ___ (due / begin) at seven. Write the complete present-tense phrase.
exercises.feedback: Is due to begin identifies the scheduled or expected start time.

exercises.prompt: The new exhibition ___ (set / open) in April. Write the complete present-tense phrase.
exercises.feedback: Is set to open expresses an arranged or expected future development.

exercises.prompt: The university ___ (look / expand) its evening courses next year. Use the present continuous with looking to.
exercises.feedback: Is looking to expand states an active institutional aim.

exercises.prompt: Correct the form: "They are on the brink to lose their licence."
acceptedAnswers: They are on the brink of losing their licence.
exercises.feedback: On the brink of must be followed by a noun or -ing form.

exercises.prompt: Correct the expected arrival time: "Our guests are due arriving before lunch."
acceptedAnswers: Our guests are due to arrive before lunch.
exercises.feedback: Scheduled expectation takes are due to + infinitive.

exercises.prompt: Correct the strong prediction: "There is certain be a delay at the checkpoint."
acceptedAnswers: There is certain to be a delay at the checkpoint.
exercises.feedback: Certain to be requires to before the infinitive. This formal certainty expression is possible with there.

exercises.prompt: Correct the intention: "The publisher is looking to releasing a digital edition."
acceptedAnswers: The publisher is looking to release a digital edition.
exercises.feedback: Looking to takes an infinitive when it means intending.

speakingExercises.prompt: Describe imminent change. Facts: The company / on the verge of / opening / a new branch. Use is.
acceptedAnswers: The company is on the verge of opening a new branch.
speakingExercises.feedback: On the verge of opening describes a development that is near.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say the expected departure time. Facts: The coach / due / leave / at six. Use a complete present-tense sentence.
acceptedAnswers: The coach is due to leave at six.
speakingExercises.feedback: Due to leave describes an expected schedule.

speakingExercises.prompt: Make a strong prediction. Facts: The proposal / bound / attract / criticism. Use is bound to.
acceptedAnswers: The proposal is bound to attract criticism.
speakingExercises.feedback: Is bound to expresses high confidence in the prediction.

speakingExercises.prompt: State an institutional intention. Facts: The library / looking / extend / its hours. Use the present continuous and full forms.
acceptedAnswers: The library is looking to extend its hours.
speakingExercises.feedback: Is looking to extend is the intended future action.

speakingExercises.prompt: Give a ready-to-happen development. Facts: The new platform / set / launch / next month. Use present be set to.
acceptedAnswers: The new platform is set to launch next month.
speakingExercises.feedback: Is set to launch conveys readiness or an expected future launch.

speakingExercises.prompt: Report a former intention without saying it happened. Facts: We / had intended / visit / the archive. Use the past perfect.
acceptedAnswers: We had intended to visit the archive.
speakingExercises.feedback: Had intended to expresses a past-held plan without guaranteeing it occurred.

speakingExercises.prompt: Correct aloud: "The director is on the point to speak."
acceptedAnswers: The director is on the point of speaking.
speakingExercises.feedback: On the point of is followed by speaking rather than to speak.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say two sentences in this order using full forms. Expected time: The debate / due / start / soon. Prediction: There / bound / be / disagreement.
acceptedAnswers: The debate is due to start soon. There is bound to be disagreement.
speakingExercises.feedback: Due to reports expected timing; bound to predicts a likely occurrence.

listeningExercises.audioText: The concert organisers say the performance is due to begin at half past seven, although the doors will open an hour earlier.
listeningExercises.prompt: What time is the performance expected to begin?
listeningExercises.feedback: Due to begin introduces the expected performance time, not the door-opening time.

listeningExercises.audioText: The rescue group has raised nearly enough money to stay open. Its director says the organisation is on the verge of reaching its target, but more donations are still needed.
listeningExercises.prompt: Has the rescue group reached its fundraising target?
choices: No, but it is very close.
No, and the group has abandoned the target.
listeningExercises.feedback: On the verge of reaching indicates closeness, not a completed achievement.

listeningExercises.audioText: The weather office expects heavy snow tonight. The roads are bound to become difficult to use.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the four-word phrase immediately after “roads”.
listeningExercises.feedback: Are bound to become is the strong future prediction spoken in the audio.

listeningExercises.audioText: The arts centre is looking to introduce evening workshops next year. The director says the idea still needs funding and has not been approved.
listeningExercises.prompt: What is the status of the evening workshops?
choices: They are an intention, not yet an approved programme.
listeningExercises.feedback: Is looking to introduce expresses a goal; the director explicitly says approval is pending.

listeningExercises.audioText: The new ferry was due to return last Friday, but a mechanical fault kept it in port. Engineers now expect it tomorrow.
listeningExercises.prompt: What happened to the original Friday schedule?
choices: The ferry was permanently withdrawn from service.
listeningExercises.feedback: Was due to return refers to an earlier expectation which the breakdown prevented.

listeningExercises.audioText: A new safety policy says that staff shall wear protective footwear inside the workshop. The supervisor explains that this is a formal rule, not merely a forecast.
listeningExercises.feedback: Shall is used here in formal regulatory language to impose an obligation.

listeningExercises.audioText: The technology company is looking to establish a regional office before the end of the year.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the four-word verb phrase immediately after “company”.
listeningExercises.feedback: This four-word phrase occurs exactly in the audio and describes an intended action.

listeningExercises.audioText: The exhibition hall is on the point of closing, so visitors should head towards the exit.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the six-word phrase immediately after “hall”.
acceptedAnswers: is on the point of closing
listeningExercises.feedback: Is on the point of closing indicates that closure is imminent.
